Ammonium bisulphite is preferred over sodium sulphite for Oman oilfield applications because of its higher reactivity at ambient temperature, lower pH effect, and lower cost per unit of oxygen removed. title: Bentonite Powder
description: Clay-based drilling mud additive for viscosity control.

details.longDescription:
Bentonite powder is sodium montmorillonite clay (CAS 1302-78-9) milled to 200 mesh, supplied by Global Chemicals LLC in API 13A drilling grade and a technical grade, in 25 kg bags and 1,000 kg big bags from stock in Muscat. The API grade is tested to the API 13A method: a viscometer dial reading of at least 30 at 600 rpm, a filtrate of 15 mL or less in 30 minutes, moisture below 12% and a fine particle size, so a drilling fluid built on it gives predictable viscosity, gel strength and filter cake from the first batch.

In water-based drilling mud, bentonite does four jobs. It builds viscosity and gel strength so the mud suspends drill cuttings and carries them to surface and holds weighting material when circulation stops. It forms a thin, low-permeability filter cake on permeable formations that limits fluid loss and supports the borehole wall. It lubricates and cools the bit, and it provides the base to which polymers, lignosulphonates and weighting agents are added. Spud muds typically run 50–70 kg of bentonite per cubic metre of fresh water; prehydrate the clay in fresh water for several hours before adding salt or other chemicals, because bentonite yields poorly in saline or hard water, and add soda ash to treat out calcium first.

Beyond the oilfield, the same clay is the slurry for diaphragm walls, bored piles and horizontal directional drilling, the grout for sealing boreholes and monitoring wells, and the liner material for ponds, lagoons and landfills, where its swelling on contact with water closes the pores of the soil. Geotechnical and water-well drillers use it at lower concentrations for the same filter-cake effect.

Bentonite is non-hazardous; the dust is a nuisance rather than a toxic hazard, so wear a mask when mixing. Keep bags dry and off the ground, because wet clay swells in the bag and will not disperse. faqs.question: What types of corrosion inhibitors are used in Oman oilfield pipelines?
faqs.answer: Oman's oilfield pipelines experience several types of corrosion requiring different inhibitor chemistries. Sweet corrosion (CO₂-dominated) is the most common in Oman's condensate-rich gas fields — organic film-forming inhibitors (imidazolines, amides, quaternary ammonium compounds) adsorb onto steel surfaces and form a protective hydrophobic barrier against carbonic acid attack. Sour corrosion (H₂S-dominated) occurs in PDO's deep gas fields — phosphate ester and film-forming amine inhibitors provide protection, but H₂S also causes hydrogen-induced cracking (HIC) and sulphide stress cracking (SSC) in high-strength steel, requiring inhibitors combined with material selection controls. Galvanic corrosion at dissimilar metal connections and under-deposit corrosion (UDC) beneath wax, scale, or sludge deposits require specialised polymeric dispersants combined with film-forming inhibitors. Global Chemicals LLC works with international inhibitor manufacturers to supply Oman oilfield-approved formulations qualified to NACE TM0197 and PDO/OQ testing protocols.

faqs.question: How are corrosion inhibitors applied in oil and gas pipelines in Oman?
faqs.answer: Corrosion inhibitors in Oman's oil and gas pipelines are applied by three primary methods: continuous injection (CI) via chemical injection quills installed at wellheads, manifolds, or platform injection points, where inhibitor is dosed proportional to production rate; batch treatment (pigging) where inhibitor solution is pigged through the pipeline as a slug to re-film internal surfaces — used for long tie-back lines or when continuous injection is impractical; and fall-back / squeeze treatment into the formation or tubing for downhole corrosion control. Continuous injection rates are calculated to maintain a minimum effective inhibitor concentration at the most corrosive point in the system (typically highest water cut, lowest temperature, highest CO₂ partial pressure). In PDO and OQ pipeline systems, inhibitor injection rates are monitored against corrosion coupons, ER (electrical resistance) probes, and chemical residual analysis to confirm protection. Global Chemicals LLC provides inhibitor design, field monitoring, and chemical supply for Oman's upstream and midstream operations.

faqs.question: What scale types are found in oilfield equipment in Oman and how are they removed?

Calcium sulphate (CaSO₄) scale (anhydrite, gypsum) is harder to dissolve and occurs where reservoir brines mix with sulphate-bearing injection water — EDTA or DTPA chelant treatments are required. Barium sulphate (BaSO₄) is the most problematic scale in Oman's commingled production wells — it is nearly insoluble in any standard acid and requires mechanical removal (coiled tubing milling) or inhibition before it forms. Iron sulphide (FeS) scale occurs in sour wells and requires specialised acid dissolvers. It reacts with dissolved oxygen to give only nitrogen and water (N2H4 + O2 → N2 + 2 H2O), so nothing accumulates in the boiler water, and its excess also helps keep the protective magnetite layer on steel in its reduced state. Dosing. The reaction consumes about 1 ppm of hydrazine per ppm of dissolved oxygen. Plants typically feed 1–2 ppm per ppm of residual oxygen after mechanical deaeration and keep a small hydrazine residual in the feedwater, measured at the economiser inlet. Reaction speed rises sharply with temperature and pH, so the feed point is normally the deaerator storage section or the boiler feed pump suction, not the cold make-up line. Catalysed grades are used where feedwater temperatures are low.

Properties. Clear, colourless liquid, specific gravity 1.03 at 20°C, boiling point 118°C for the monohydrate. Miscible with water in all proportions and strongly alkaline.

Handling. Hydrazine is toxic, corrosive and classified as a suspected carcinogen. faqs.question: What is MDEA and how is it used for gas sweetening in Oman?
faqs.answer: MDEA (methyl diethanolamine) is a tertiary alkanolamine used as the primary solvent in gas sweetening (acid gas removal) units in Oman's oil and gas processing plants. Gas sweetening removes hydrogen sulphide (H₂S) and carbon dioxide (CO₂) from sour natural gas and associated gas before export, LNG production, or injection. MDEA selectively absorbs H₂S over CO₂ at standard operating conditions (40–60°C, 5–70 bar), making it preferred where H₂S removal is the primary objective and CO₂ slip is acceptable — as in many Oman PDO gas fields. The absorbed H₂S is released by heating the rich MDEA solvent in a regenerator (stripper) at 120–130°C, regenerating lean MDEA for recirculation. MDEA is preferred over MEA (monoethanolamine) because it has lower solvent degradation, lower corrosion rates, lower energy consumption for regeneration, and higher H₂S loading capacity. faqs.question: What is the MDEA concentration typically used in gas sweetening units in Oman?

At concentrations below 35%, absorption capacity is reduced, requiring higher circulation rates and larger equipment. Above 50%, solvent viscosity increases at low temperatures, and corrosion rates accelerate under high H₂S and CO₂ loading. The exact concentration is set during plant design based on gas composition, inlet H₂S content, target outlet specification, and operating pressure. Oman PDO gas specifications require pipeline gas to contain less than 4 ppm H₂S and less than 2% CO₂ vol/vol. For plants treating very high H₂S concentrations (above 10% v/v in feed), enhanced MDEA formulations with activator additives (piperazine, triethanolamine) are used to accelerate mass transfer. faqs.question: What is MEG (monoethylene glycol) used for in oil and gas operations in Oman?
faqs.answer: MEG (monoethylene glycol, ethylene glycol) is a primary hydrate inhibitor and gas dehydration chemical used extensively in Oman's oil and gas sector by PDO, OQ, and BP Oman. In subsea and deepwater gas pipelines, hydrates — ice-like crystalline structures of water and gas molecules — can form at high pressure and low temperature, blocking flow lines and creating serious safety hazards. MEG is injected at the wellhead and into pipeline risers to depress the hydrate formation temperature (thermodynamic inhibition), keeping the gas stream in the hydrate-free zone throughout transport. MEG is also used as a dehydration solvent in glycol contactors to remove water vapour from natural gas before export. In Oman's onshore gas fields, MEG injection is standard practice in wet gas gathering systems, condensate lines, and LNG feed gas conditioning. Global Chemicals LLC supplies technical-grade and recovered MEG in bulk and IBC quantities for Oman's oilfield operations.

faqs.question: How does MEG compare to TEG for gas dehydration in Oman oil and gas operations?
faqs.answer: MEG (monoethylene glycol) and TEG (triethylene glycol) are both hygroscopic glycols used for gas dehydration, but they differ significantly in physical properties and applications. TEG has a much higher boiling point (285°C vs MEG's 197°C) and lower vapour pressure, making it superior for deep dehydration in gas processing plants — TEG can achieve dew point depressions of 40–60°C in standard gas-glycol contactors, meeting pipeline water content specifications. MEG is preferred for direct injection into pipelines and wellheads as a flow assurance chemical rather than a bulk dehydration solvent, because its lower molecular weight means lower injection volumes per mole of water removed. In Oman, TEG is the standard dehydration medium in gas processing plants at Saih Rawl, Harweel, and Khazzan, while MEG injection is used in wet gathering lines and multiphase flow lines where TEG contactors are impractical. faqs.question: How is methanol used as a hydrate inhibitor in Oman oil and gas operations?
faqs.answer: Methanol (methyl alcohol, CH₃OH) is a thermodynamic hydrate inhibitor injected into oil and gas flow lines, wellheads, and subsea pipelines to prevent gas hydrate formation. Hydrates form when water and light hydrocarbons (methane, ethane, propane) combine at high pressure and low temperature, creating solid crystalline plugs that block pipelines and can cause blowout hazards during depressurisation. Methanol works by dissolving in the aqueous phase and lowering the water activity, which shifts the hydrate equilibrium curve to lower temperatures, keeping the system in the hydrate-free zone. Typical injection concentrations are 20–50 wt% methanol in the aqueous phase, depending on temperature and pressure. Methanol is preferred over glycols (MEG, DEG) in subsea and offshore applications where regeneration is impractical because methanol losses in the gas phase are accepted as an operating cost. details.longDescription:

Global Chemicals LLC supplies it at 99.0% minimum purity by GC, about 38% sulphur, density 1.00 g/cm³, boiling point 121 °C and flash point 13 °C, in sealed 208 L steel drums under a nitrogen blanket, with a batch certificate of analysis, to gas-distribution companies, city-gas projects and industrial fuel-gas operators across Oman and the GCC.

Why THT. Natural gas has no smell, and regulations require it to be detectable by smell at a fraction of the lower flammability limit, typically one fifth. Odorants are either mercaptan blends or THT. THT is chosen for pipeline networks because it resists oxidation, is not adsorbed by soil or pipe wall to the same degree as mercaptans, and therefore holds a consistent odour intensity along long distribution runs and at the far ends of new networks; its smell is distinctive and does not fade in the pipe. Typical dosing runs at 10–25 mg of THT per cubic metre of gas, set by the regulator's detectability requirement and confirmed by sniff tests or a THT analyser at the network extremities. It is injected by a dosing skid proportional to the gas flow, or by a wick or bypass odoriser on small systems; the oilfield chemicals guide linked on this page covers related products.

Other uses: odorising fuel gas and process gas for leak detection in industrial plants, biogas and syngas before grid injection, and LPG where the specification calls for THT rather than ethyl mercaptan.

Handling: THT is a flammable liquid (UN 2412, Class 3) with an intense, penetrating odour; the smallest spill or vapour release triggers gas-leak reports across a neighbourhood. Keep drums sealed and nitrogen-blanketed until use, transfer with closed, earthed systems into the odoriser tank, store in a ventilated, shaded, bunded area away from ignition sources, and keep a sodium hypochlorite solution ready to oxidise and neutralise spills and contaminated PPE.
